When a necessary constraint meets an operation that cannot easily stop, the most useful step is usually to plan the constraint around the customer's operation with the people who run it. Insisting on the plan as written, or redesigning it at great cost before asking, both skip that conversation.
questions.mindset: Fit unavoidable disruption around how the customer actually works, and plan it with them.

questions.stem: Your team is building a training platform for a pharmaceutical company. Its learning and development director, the main customer stakeholder, has missed the last three sprint reviews. She now asks for an emailed summary instead, saying the reviews take two hours and she is busy with an audit until the end of the quarter. Five sprints remain, and two of them deliver the assessment features she asked for most. Which two actions should you take?

options.text: Agree with her which of the remaining reviews will show the assessment features, and book short, focused sessions with her for those reviews now.
options.rationale: Her time is scarce, so it goes on the work she cares about most. A short session on those increments keeps her judgement where it matters without asking for two hours.

options.text: Offer her a short recorded walkthrough of each increment, with two or three specific questions she can answer in writing when she has time.
options.rationale: A recording lets her see working software on her own schedule, and pointed questions draw out real feedback rather than general approval.

options.text: Send the emailed summary she has asked for after each review, listing what was completed and asking her to raise any concerns by reply.
options.rationale: The candidate gives the customer exactly what she asked for. A list of completed items does not let her see the product, so silence will be taken as approval it is not.

options.text: Ask the product owner to accept the assessment features on her behalf until the audit ends, so that the team is not held up waiting for her views.
options.rationale: The candidate replaces the customer's judgement with a proxy on the very features she cares about most, which is where a mismatch would cost the most.

options.text: Move the assessment features into the final sprint, after the audit ends, so that she can attend that review in person and give her feedback directly.
options.rationale: The candidate protects her attendance by delaying feedback to the end, when any rework on her priority features has no sprint left to happen in.

questions.explanation: When a key customer cannot keep up with the team's feedback cadence, the aim is to keep their judgement in the loop at the points where it matters most, in a form they can actually give. That usually means fitting the format to the customer's constraints and concentrating their time on the work they care about, rather than accepting a channel that cannot carry real feedback or handing their judgement to someone else.
questions.mindset: Adapt how the customer gives feedback, but keep their feedback on the work that matters to them.

questions.stem: Your agile team works on a time-and-materials contract for a payments start-up, billed at €52,000 a month. After six months, the start-up's finance director tells you the forecast cost to finish the backlog is far higher than she expected. She had assumed velocity would keep rising, so each month would deliver more for the same money. The founder, who agreed the contract, has never raised cost. Which two actions should you take?

options.text: Explain to her how the team's velocity has behaved and why it has levelled off, and walk through the current forecast cost to finish with her.
options.rationale: Her expectation came from an assumption about velocity that nobody corrected. Showing her how it has actually behaved replaces the assumption with evidence.

options.text: Agree with her and the founder to show spend to date and the forecast cost to finish, as a range, at every sprint review from now on.
options.rationale: A routine view of spend and forecast stops the next assumption forming. Both the finance director and the founder see the same numbers at the same time.

options.text: Ask the team to look for ways to raise velocity over the next three sprints, so that the forecast moves closer to what the finance director expected.
options.rationale: The candidate chases an expectation built on a misunderstanding. Pressure on velocity tends to inflate estimates or cut quality rather than deliver more.

options.text: Refer her to the founder, who agreed the time-and-materials terms, since cost expectations under the contract are a matter for the start-up to settle internally.
options.rationale: The candidate treats the issue as the client's internal business. Her expectation rested on delivery data the team holds, so the team is best placed to correct it.

options.text: Propose converting the remaining backlog to a fixed-price contract, so that the finance director has the cost certainty she evidently expected from the start.
options.rationale: The candidate assumes certainty is what she wants. Fixing the price of an emergent backlog adds a risk premium and solves a problem she has not raised.

questions.explanation: Customers fill gaps in what they are shown with assumptions, and a common one on time-and-materials work is that the team will keep speeding up. Expectations about cost stay realistic only when the customer routinely sees spend and the forecast to finish, explained in terms of how the team's delivery rate actually behaves. Changing the commercial model or pushing the team faster responds to the symptom rather than the missing information.
questions.mindset: Keep the cost forecast in front of the customer, so their assumptions never have to fill the gap.

questions.stem: You are managing a £3.1 million extension to a secondary school, built while the school stays open. The contract allows noisy work from 8am to 6pm on weekdays, and your site complies. The head teacher writes to complain that drilling is disrupting lessons, and that GCSE exams start in five weeks. She says she expected the contractor to work around the school day. Which two actions should you take?

options.text: Meet the head teacher to find out which rooms, lessons and exam sessions are most affected, and when quieter working would matter most to the school.
options.rationale: The complaint is real but not yet specific. Knowing exactly which rooms and times matter is what lets the work be reshaped without stopping it.

options.text: Re-plan the noisiest activities into the windows the school identifies, such as half-term and late afternoons, and confirm the revised plan with her in writing.
options.rationale: Re-sequencing within the permitted hours meets the school's need at little cost, and confirming it in writing gives the head teacher something she can rely on.

options.text: Reply that the site is working within the hours the contract allows, and offer to share the noise-monitoring results with the school each week from now on.
options.rationale: The candidate answers a complaint about lessons with evidence of compliance. The school's expectation was about its teaching, which the data does nothing to protect.

options.text: Pause all noisy work until the exams finish, accepting the schedule delay, so that the school cannot be disrupted during its most sensitive period.
options.rationale: The candidate reacts with a blanket stop before learning which periods matter. The delay may cost far more than a targeted re-plan and the school may not want it.

options.text: Refer the complaint to the local authority's contract manager, who signed the contract, and ask whether the working hours should be formally varied.
options.rationale: The candidate reaches for formal change when the sequencing of work inside the agreed hours is already the project manager's to adjust.

questions.explanation: Meeting the contract is the minimum, and on a site shared with a live operation the customer's real expectation is that the work fits around what they are doing. The useful response finds out precisely which activities and times matter and reshapes the work within the agreed limits, so the customer's priorities are protected without unnecessary cost. Pointing to compliance, or reacting with a blanket stop, both avoid learning what the customer actually needs.
questions.mindset: Comply with the contract, then fit the work around what the customer is trying to do.

questions.stem: During planning for a payroll replacement at a retail group, the client's finance team states three expectations. Match each expectation to the place in the project's documentation where it should be captured so that it can be tracked. One choice is not used.

prompts.text: The monthly payroll run for 18,000 staff must complete within two hours of being started.
Processing costs should fall by 30% within nine months of go-live, as the business case promised.
The finance director wants to hear within two working days if the forecast cost rises by more than 5%.

options.text: A non-functional requirement with a measurable acceptance criterion
options.rationale: A performance expectation becomes trackable when it is written as a requirement with a test the delivered system can pass or fail at acceptance.

options.text: The benefits management plan, with an owner and measurement dates
options.rationale: A cost saving after go-live is an outcome, not a deliverable. It needs an owner and dates for measurement, which is what the benefits plan provides.

options.text: The communications management plan, as an escalation trigger
options.rationale: An expectation about being told, by when and at what threshold, is a communication commitment. Writing it as a trigger makes it something the project checks every reporting cycle.

options.text: The change log, as an approved change to the baseline
options.rationale: Not used. None of these alters an agreed baseline; they are expectations being captured at planning, before there is a baseline to change.

questions.explanation: An expectation can only be tracked once it is written where the project already looks for that kind of commitment. Performance expectations become testable requirements, outcome expectations become benefits with owners and dates, and expectations about being kept informed become part of the communication approach. An expectation left only in meeting notes is likely to be rediscovered at acceptance, when it is most expensive to meet.
questions.mindset: Write each customer expectation where the project will check it, not where it was first heard.

questions.stem: A housing association's repairs service is being redesigned by a hybrid team, and the association wants evidence of how well it meets tenants' expectations. Match each question the association wants answered to the measure that best answers it. One choice is not used.

prompts.text: Were tenants satisfied with how their individual repair was handled once the job was closed?
How much effort did tenants have to put in to report a repair through the new online form?
Would tenants recommend the association's repairs service to a friend moving into social housing?

options.text: A short satisfaction rating sent after each completed job
options.rationale: A transactional rating taken straight after the job captures how that one interaction felt, while the tenant still remembers it.

options.text: A customer effort score asked straight after the form is submitted
options.rationale: Effort scores ask how easy a specific task was. Asking at the moment of submission ties the answer to the form rather than to the repair that follows.

options.text: A likelihood-to-recommend score from a periodic tenant survey
options.rationale: Likelihood to recommend reflects the tenant's view of the service as a whole, which is best asked periodically rather than after a single job.

options.text: Weekly counts of repairs reported online compared with by phone
options.rationale: Not used. Channel counts show what tenants did, not how they felt. Tenants may use the form because the phone line is busy, not because it meets their expectations.

questions.explanation: Each satisfaction measure answers a different question: how a single interaction felt, how hard a task was, or how the customer regards the relationship overall. Choosing the measure means deciding first which expectation is being tested and at what point in the customer's experience. Behavioural data such as usage is useful alongside these, but it records what customers did, not whether their expectations were met.
questions.mindset: Pick the measure for the question about expectations you are trying to answer.

questions.stem: An agile team is building a membership app for a network of sports clubs. Complete each sentence with who should take the customer's request, so that it is handled by the person or forum that owns it. One choice is not used.

prompts.text: Midway through a sprint, the clubs' membership lead asks for an urgent new story to replace one the team has already started. The request should go to
During a review, the membership lead points out that a story being demonstrated does not meet one of the acceptance criteria agreed for it. The request should go to
The clubs' procurement officer asks for the day rates in the contract to be reduced for the next phase of work. The request should go to

options.text: the product owner, who decides with the team whether to change the sprint
options.rationale: Swapping work in a running sprint changes what the team is building and why. That trade-off belongs to the product owner, with the team advising on what it would disrupt.

options.text: the development team, which keeps the story open as not done and fixes it
options.rationale: A story that misses an agreed criterion is unfinished, not changed. It stays with the team as incomplete work rather than becoming a new request to prioritise.

options.text: the supplier's commercial manager, who owns the contract terms
options.rationale: Day rates are a commercial term outside the delivery team's authority. Routing the request to the contract owner gets the client a real answer.

options.text: the scrum master, who decides how customer requests are prioritised
options.rationale: Not used. The scrum master facilitates and coaches but owns neither the backlog's priorities nor the contract, so a request routed there has to be passed on again.

questions.explanation: Customer requests on an agile project arrive through many channels, but each kind has an owner: changes to what the team is working on belong to the product owner, work that fails its agreed criteria stays with the team as unfinished, and commercial terms sit outside the team altogether. Routing a request correctly is what lets the customer get a real answer rather than a sympathetic one from someone who cannot give it.
questions.mindset: Before answering a customer's request, ask who actually owns the answer.

questions.stem: An online grocer's operations director is about to sign a hosting contract offering 99.5% monthly availability. She says this matches her expectation of 'no more than about 20 minutes of downtime a month'. Using a 30-day month, work out what the contract allows and what her expectation would actually require.

blanks.label: Downtime allowed by 99.5% availability in a 30-day month, in minutes
blanks.rationale: A 30-day month has 30 × 24 × 60 = 43,200 minutes. 0.5% of 43,200 is 216 minutes, about three and a half hours, which is more than ten times her expectation.

blanks.label: Availability needed for no more than 20 minutes of downtime in a 30-day month, as a percentage to two decimal places
blanks.rationale: (43,200 − 20) ÷ 43,200 = 0.99954, or 99.95%. Her expectation needs roughly 'three and a half nines', not the 99.5% she is about to sign.

questions.explanation: Customers often express expectations in everyday terms and then agree to figures that sound close but mean something quite different. Converting a percentage into the quantity the customer will actually experience, such as minutes of downtime, shows whether the number and the expectation match before either side is bound by it. The time to test that is before signature, because afterwards the gap becomes a dispute.
questions.mindset: Translate a customer's numbers into what they will experience before agreeing them.

questions.stem: You are delivering a warehouse automation project for a pharmaceutical distributor. The diagram is a timeline of the monthly customer reviews, showing the client's satisfaction score and a note from each meeting. In month 8 the client formally complained that operator training was late. Select the earliest month at which you should have acted on the client's training expectation.

graphic.title: Timeline of monthly customer reviews, months 4 to 8, with satisfaction scores and meeting notes
graphic.caption: Select a month. Use Tab or the arrow keys to move between months, then Enter or Space.

regions.label: Month 4 — score 4.3. Client asks for shorter review meetings.
regions.rationale: This is a real expectation, but about meetings rather than training. The candidate picks the earliest note without checking whether it relates to the later complaint.

regions.label: Month 5 — score 4.2. Client asks when the operator training plan will be issued.
regions.rationale: The first question about training is the first sign of what the client is waiting for. Answering it with a plan and a date then would have shaped the expectation before it hardened.

regions.label: Month 6 — score 4.2. Client asks again about training; its go-live shift rota is being set.
regions.rationale: The signal is now unmistakable, but it is the second time of asking and the client is already planning its rota without the information. The candidate waits for repetition before acting.

regions.label: Month 7 — score 3.6. Client's operations manager is quieter than usual and raises no questions.
regions.rationale: The candidate waits for the score to move. Satisfaction scores lag behind expectations, and a customer who stops asking may simply have stopped expecting an answer.

regions.label: Month 8 — score 2.9. Formal complaint that operator training is late.
regions.rationale: A formal complaint confirms that the expectation has already been missed. The candidate treats the escalation as the trigger, when it is the result of earlier signals going unanswered.

questions.explanation: Customer expectations usually show up first as questions and requests, well before they appear in a satisfaction score, which tends to move only once the customer already feels let down. The earliest point to act is the first time the customer signals what they are waiting for, because that is when a date or a plan can still shape the expectation. Scores and complaints confirm a problem; questions predict one.
questions.mindset: Treat a customer's question as an early signal of an expectation, not as routine traffic.
